newsitem.title: ANGOLA: FEATURE - Angolan fishermen say oil firm polluting beaches.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Angolan fishermen say oil firm polluting beaches.

text.p: Jose Vasconcelas has made his living for most of his life from the sea off Angola's oil-rich Cabinda enclave.

He says his catches have never been so meagre as they are now. The fishermen blame the Cabinda Gulf Oil Company (Cabgoc), a subsidiary of U.S.-based Chevron, which runs the oil platforms off the Cabinda coast.
"Fishing used to be so easy and so good here, but just look at this pitiful catch," says Vasconcelas, 36, gesturing to a pile of palm-size flounder, tiny shrimp and immature crabs.
"This is what we have caught since daylight this morning. There is some sort of crisis in the sea and we think it comes from all the pollution in the water," he says.
The enclave, home to around 300,000 people, is separated from the rest of Angola by a sliver of land from Zaire and the Congo river.
The fishermen accuse Cabgoc of fouling the waters with pollution from the offshore drilling and say it has turned the beaches black.
"Those beaches have not always been black," said Catholic priest Jorge Congo, an outspoken critic of the offshore drilling activities.
Cabinda environmental group Gremio says although it does not have scientific evidence of pollution, it is convinced the sea is becoming more polluted.
"The ecological balance here has been upset by the oil pollution," said Gremio leader Agostinho Chicaia.
"You can see evidence of this all along the coast. I have lived here all my life."
OIL COMPANY BLAMES BACTERIA, NOT POLLUTION
But Chevron says the black beaches are not due to pollution but rather to bacteria in the sand.
A recent study funded by Cabinda Gulf found that any contamination of the water and beaches "was well below the level that would adversely affect the environment".
Cabgoc is in partnership with Angola's state oil company Sonangol, French company Elf Aquitaine and the Italian company Agip.

Cabgoc and its partners, often referred to as the Cabinda Association, produce more than 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day which accounts for three-quarters of Angola's total annual oil output worth more than $4 billion.
"I suppose if I were a fisherman in Cabinda I would deal with it the same way," said Antonio Palmeirim, Chevron's director of public relations in Angola.

"But the truth is the results of the study say there is not enough pollution to harm the environment," he said. "And these black sands everyone in Cabinda talks about are due to bacteria, not to oil pollution."
The Chevron study was carried out by the Swiss enviromental firm Woodward and Clyde in late 1995 and 1996.

Even though the study has been completed and the results are known by company officials, Palmeirim declined to release the data until a memorandum, now circulating among members of the Angolan government and its partners, was signed by all of the parties.
Cabinda has been the scene for several years of a small-scale war between separatist guerrillas and the Angolan government over independence.
FLEC (Front for the Liberation of the Cabinda Enclave) complains that the enclave alone generates over 60 percent of the entire country's oil output yet it gets little benefit in return.
